items.headline: A new piano drama is airing this week
items.body: "Four Hands, Two Sonatas" runs on tvN with Song Kang and Lee Jun Young as two arts-school students who become friends and rivals. If you are building a watch list, this is the one starting now.

items.headline: You still do not need a K-ETA — but you do need the arrival card
items.body: Travellers from 22 countries, including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan, stay exempt from K-ETA until 31 December 2026. Most visitors now submit a digital e-Arrival Card before flying instead.

items.headline: Water is free, and you usually pour it yourself
items.body: In most Korean restaurants water and the small side dishes come free, and refills are free too. Look for the water jug and cups stacked near the door or on a shelf — staff will not bring them to you.

items.headline: Autumn leaves will come late this year — Seoraksan turns on 3 October
items.body: The Korea Tourism Organization’s 2026 forecast puts the first colour on Seoraksan on 3 October, with the peak around 25 October, and Bukhansan above Seoul peaking about 4 November. If you are planning a mountain trip, mid-October to early November is the window — the dates move with the weather.

items.headline: Since 2023 Korea counts age the way everyone else does
items.body: Until June 2023 many Koreans gave their “Korean age”, which could run a year or two higher than their international age. Documents and the law now use only international age (만 나이), though you will still hear the old way in casual talk — so “how old are you?” can get two answers.

items.headline: Chuseok is next week — book trains and hotels now
items.body: Chuseok, the harvest holiday, falls on Friday 25 September; the official holiday runs Thursday 24 to Saturday 26, so most people are off through Sunday. Offices and many small restaurants close, while the subway, convenience stores, malls and big sights stay open. KTX seats and central hotels sell out first.

items.headline: Songpyeon: the half-moon rice cake families make for Chuseok
items.body: Songpyeon are small rice cakes filled with sesame, chestnut or sweet beans and steamed on a bed of pine needles, which is where the name comes from. Families traditionally shape them together the night before Chuseok, and every market and department store is full of them this week.

items.headline: Read outdoors in the middle of Seoul — free, Fridays to Sundays
items.body: The Seoul Outdoor Library puts out beanbags and thousands of books on Seoul Plaza, Gwanghwamun Square and along Cheonggyecheon every Friday to Sunday until 1 November. No ticket and no library card — sit down and stay as long as you like.

items.headline: One card for every bus, subway and taxi
items.body: A T-money card from any convenience store works on public transport nationwide and gives you the transfer discount, so a bus-to-subway trip costs less than two separate fares. Top it up in cash at the store or at the machines in subway stations.

items.headline: “The Scandal” lands on Netflix today
items.body: Son Ye Jin and Ji Chang Wook lead this Joseon-era romance, a period retelling of Dangerous Liaisons with Nana in the cast. It is a full historical drama — palaces, hanbok and the formal speech you hear in sageuk.

items.headline: What Chuseok actually is
items.body: Chuseok is the harvest festival on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month. Families gather, set a table of food for their ancestors and visit the family graves — the closest thing Korea has to Thanksgiving, and the one week a year when Seoul empties out.

items.headline: A free orchestra concert in the park tonight
items.body: The Seoul Philharmonic plays outdoors at Seoul Children’s Grand Park from 7 pm to 8:20 pm — no ticket, no reservation. Bring a mat and arrive as the sun goes down.

items.headline: Guro’s Asian culture festival runs this weekend along Anyangcheon
items.body: The Guro G Festival fills the stream banks between Gocheokgyo and Ogeumgyo bridges with food, stalls and performances from across Asia on 19 and 20 September. Take Line 1 to Guro or Line 2 to Guro Digital Complex.

items.headline: The Seoul Autumn Festival starts tomorrow and runs to 29 November
items.body: Two months of open-air events across the city, from riverside shows on the Hangang to the fireworks festival in October. The city government’s English site posts each week’s line-up.

items.headline: The one Chuseok greeting you can say to anyone
items.body: “추석 잘 보내세요” — have a good Chuseok — works for a shopkeeper, a colleague or a host family. Drop the ending for friends: “추석 잘 보내”. Say it any time this week; nobody waits for the day itself.

items.headline: Andong’s mask dance festival opens Thursday and runs through Chuseok
items.body: The Andong International Mask Dance Festival runs 24 September to 4 October at Talchum Park and around Andong station, with the Hahoe village mask dance at its centre. Andong is about two and a half hours from Seoul by train, which makes it a natural holiday trip.

items.headline: Busan’s film festival is 6–15 October
items.body: The 31st Busan International Film Festival runs for ten days around the Busan Cinema Center, with more than three hundred films and dozens of world premieres. Popular screenings sell out within minutes of tickets opening, so watch the official site.

items.headline: Forty years of a textile pioneer go on show today at the craft museum
items.body: The Seoul Museum of Craft Art opens “Equinox: Autumn and Spring” on Tuesday 22 September, a retrospective of Chang Eung-bok, one of Korea’s first-generation textile designers. It is free, on the third floor of Exhibition Building 1, and stays up until 7 March 2027 — Tuesday to Sunday, 10 am to 6 pm, closed Mondays.

items.headline: Roads out of Seoul jam from Wednesday afternoon — here is when to move
items.body: Half the country heads to its 고향, the family hometown, this week. TMAP’s forecast puts the worst traffic out of Seoul on Wednesday afternoon and Thursday — a drive to Daejeon that normally takes under three hours is expected to take over four at 3 pm on Wednesday — and the heaviest traffic back into Seoul on Chuseok Day itself, Friday 25 September, from 8 am. If you are driving, Saturday and Sunday are the quieter days.

items.headline: Every royal palace in Seoul is free from Thursday to Sunday
items.body: Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, Deoksugung and Changgyeonggung, plus Jongmyo Shrine and the Joseon royal tombs, waive admission from 24 to 27 September with no closing day. Jongmyo, normally a timed guided tour only, can be wandered freely, and the guard-changing ceremony at Gyeongbokgung runs at 10 am and 2 pm with no booking. Changdeokgung’s Secret Garden is the one exception and still needs its own ticket.

items.headline: Why every supermarket is stacked with boxes of Spam this week
items.body: Koreans give gift sets to relatives, friends and business contacts before Chuseok, and companies hand them to staff. Fruit, health supplements and beef top the surveys, but the flat boxes of canned ham, tuna and cooking oil are the ones that surprise visitors — canned ham has been a holiday gift since the 1980s, and about 60 percent of Spam sales come from the two big holidays. Stores clear whole aisles for them one to two weeks ahead.

items.headline: Namsangol Hanok Village throws a three-day Chuseok festival from Friday
items.body: Namsan Dalbit Madang runs Friday to Sunday, 25–27 September, 10 am to 8 pm, in the old houses of Namsangol Hanok Village near Chungmuro station. Expect traditional performances, hanbok to try on, old-fashioned games and a Korean food market. Entry is free; some activities and food are charged.

items.headline: Museums are free this holiday — but most close on Chuseok Day itself
items.body: The National Museum of Korea opens on 24, 26 and 27 September with free traditional music and dance performances each day, and all four MMCA branches are free for the whole four-day break. The National Museum, the National Folk Museum and MMCA Seoul close on Friday 25 September, so make Thursday or the weekend your museum day. The Folk Museum’s “All Together for Hangawi” adds ssireum wrestling and jegichagi, a game a bit like hacky sack.

items.headline: Tonight’s Chuseok moon rises over Seoul at 5:34 pm
items.body: Chuseok falls on the full moon of the eighth lunar month, and going out to look at it is part of the day. In Seoul the moon comes up at about 5:34 pm on Friday and 5:59 pm on Saturday — but it is only perfectly full at 1:49 am on Sunday, so Saturday night is the rounder one if you want a photo.

items.headline: Jeon: the pan-fried slices that fill every Chuseok kitchen
items.body: Jeon are slices of meat, vegetables or seafood coated in flour and egg and fried in a shallow pan, and the smell of them frying is the smell of the holiday. Families make stacks for the ancestral table and eat the rest for days. They are on restaurant menus year-round too — look for 모둠전, an assorted plate.

items.headline: Try tuho and jegichagi at two Seoul museums today
items.body: The Seoul Baekje Museum in Olympic Park holds its Chuseok festival on Saturday 26 September from 10 am to 5 pm, with performances, hands-on crafts and traditional games. Across town the Seoul Urban Life Museum runs gugak music, a magic show, tuho arrow-tossing, jegichagi and pouch-making from 1 to 5 pm. Both are free.

items.headline: Hangawi: the other name for Chuseok
items.body: You will see 한가위 on banners and hear it in greetings this week. It is the older, native-Korean name for the holiday, literally “the great middle” of autumn — the full moon in the middle of the eighth lunar month. 추석 is the Sino-Korean name; both mean the same day, and “즐거운 한가위 보내세요” works just as well as the Chuseok version.

items.headline: “Four Hands, Two Sonatas” plays its last episode next Sunday
items.body: Song Kang’s piano drama reaches its finale on Netflix on Sunday 4 October, with new episodes still landing on Saturdays and Sundays until then — this is the week to catch up. The next weekly K-dramas follow straight after: the medical remake “Doctor X” from 9 October and the colonial-era spy drama “100 Days of Deception” from 10 October.

items.headline: 1330: the number to call when you are stuck
items.body: The Korea Travel Helpline answers on 1330 — from abroad +82-2-1330 — for anything from a lost bag to which bus to take, and it also has a text chat in Korean, English, Japanese, Chinese, Russian, Vietnamese, Thai and Indonesian. Save it now: on a holiday, when many shops are shut, it is the quickest way to find out what is open.

items.headline: Suwon’s fortress walls are lit up every night this week — last show Tuesday 6 October
items.body: The Suwon Hwaseong Media Art show projects light and story onto Hwaseomun Gate, Janganmun Gate and Jangan Park from 6 pm to 10 pm nightly until 6 October, with a media park of installations, photo spots and food stalls between the gates. Suwon is on subway Line 1 south of Seoul, so it works as an evening trip; go on a weeknight if you want it quiet.

items.headline: How to get a train seat: sales open a month ahead at 7 am
items.body: KTX and other Korail tickets go on sale one month before departure at 7 am, and can be bought at the station, on the Korail website, the KORAIL+ app, Naver or KakaoT right up to departure. Visitors can also buy a Korail Pass — 2, 3, 4 or 5 days of unlimited standard-class travel within ten days. The English help line is +82-1599-7777, 8 am to 8 pm.

items.headline: Fifty gardens made by Seoul residents open in Yangjae on Thursday
items.body: The autumn edition of the Seoul International Garden Show opens on 1 October at Maehun Citizen’s Forest in Yangjae and runs to 27 October, this time with about fifty gardens designed and planted by residents rather than professionals. There are guided garden walks each day and an outdoor “forest cinema” on the forest stage on weekend evenings from 7 to 9 pm.

items.headline: Press the button, not the waiter — and do not leave a tip
items.body: Most Korean restaurant tables have a call button; press it and a server comes, so nobody is being ignored while you wait to catch an eye. If there is no button, a clear “저기요” does the same job. Spoons and chopsticks are usually in a drawer built into the table, refills of water and side dishes are free, and tipping is neither required nor expected.

items.headline: A three-day weekend is coming: National Foundation Day falls on Saturday, so Monday is off
items.body: Gaecheonjeol on 3 October marks the founding of the first Korean kingdom by the legendary Dangun, and because it lands on a Saturday this year, Monday 5 October is a substitute public holiday. Banks, offices and government counters close on Monday; shops, restaurants and transport run as normal, and the palaces and big sights stay open. Trains out of Seoul for the long weekend fill up early, so book now.

items.headline: A national park inside the city: hiking is Seoul’s weekend religion
items.body: Bukhansan, the highest mountain in Seoul, is one of the few national parks in the world that sits inside a city, and on an autumn weekend its trails are packed with hikers in full kit. You do not need your own gear — the Seoul Hiking Tourism Center near Bukhansan Ui station rents boots, jackets, poles and gloves. The ritual is gimbap and cup ramyeon at the top, then jeon and makgeolli at the bottom.

items.headline: Sixty years of a media-art pioneer opens today at the Seoul Museum of Art
items.body: The Seoul Museum of Art’s Seosomun main building, a short walk from City Hall station, opens a retrospective of Lynn Hershman Leeson on Thursday 1 October — the American artist and film-maker who has been making work about identity, screens and machines since the 1960s. It is her first museum solo show in Asia and stays up until 7 February 2027.

items.headline: The convenience store is also a kitchen
items.body: Korean convenience stores are open around the clock, and most have a counter with hot water, a microwave and often a ramyeon cooker so you can eat what you just bought. The CU near Hongik University takes it furthest with a “Ramyun Library” of about 105 kinds of instant noodle, labelled in English with spice levels; you pay for the noodles plus a 900-won paper bowl and cook them yourself at the machine.

items.headline: Jinju’s river fills with lanterns from Saturday
items.body: The Jinju Namgang Yudeung Festival runs from 3 to 18 October around Jinjuseong Fortress and the Namgang river, with the lanterns lit from 6 pm to midnight every night. The custom goes back to the 1592 siege of the fortress, when defenders floated lanterns on the river to block the enemy at night and to send word to their families outside the walls; today thousands of them float on the Namgang and line the fortress.

items.headline: Two towns share a 1,500-year-old kingdom for nine days from Saturday
items.body: The 72nd Baekje Cultural Festival runs 3 to 11 October in Buyeo and Gongju, the two old capitals of the Baekje kingdom in South Chungcheong. Buyeo stages its programme around the Jeongnimsa temple site and the town centre; Gongju opens on Saturday at 7 pm with a show of a thousand drones over Geumgang Singwan Park, and its events run along the river and up to Gongsanseong Fortress.

items.headline: A king rides to Suwon tomorrow — the royal procession re-enactment is on Sunday
items.body: Every autumn Seoul, Gyeonggi, Suwon and Hwaseong jointly re-stage King Jeongjo’s 1795 procession to his father’s tomb, and this year it is Sunday 4 October. The Suwon leg leaves the Nosong pine belt, passes the sports complex and Janganmun Gate and ends at Hwaseong Haenggung plaza, as a costumed procession with a citizens’ parade alongside. The Suwon Hwaseong Cultural Festival opens the same day and runs at the fortress until 11 October.

items.headline: Why Hangul can be learned in an afternoon
items.body: King Sejong had the alphabet created in 1443 and proclaimed it in 1446 in a book called Hunminjeongeum, “the proper sounds for instructing the people”, so that ordinary Koreans would not have to learn Chinese characters. It has just 14 consonants and 10 vowels, stacked into syllable blocks, and literacy rose sharply once it spread. The original book is a national treasure and on UNESCO’s Memory of the World register.

items.headline: Next Friday is Hangul Day — and this year it is the hundredth
items.body: Hangul Day on Friday 9 October is a public holiday marking the alphabet’s proclamation in 1446, which makes 2026 the 580th anniversary — and the 100th Hangul Day, first kept in 1926. The National Hangeul Museum has called this the “Year of Hangeul”, with a Hangeul Hanmadang festival of performances and hands-on activities on Gwanghwamun Square on the day itself. If you are learning the alphabet, this is the week to be seen doing it.

items.headline: The palaces open at night from Wednesday for the autumn Royal Culture Festival
items.body: The autumn K-Royal Culture Festival runs 7 to 11 October across Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, Deoksugung, Changgyeonggung and Jongmyo Shrine, with daytime tours and workshops and evening performances against the lit-up palaces. It opens a day early with a free KBS “Immortal Songs” concert on Tuesday 6 October at 5 pm on the Heungnyemun plaza of Gyeongbokgung, though seats went by advance registration. Some festival programmes are free, others need a ticket — check the festival site.

items.headline: Busan’s film festival opens tomorrow and runs for ten days
items.body: The 31st Busan International Film Festival runs from 6 to 15 October around the Busan Cinema Center in Haeundae. This year it adds a competition section for the first time, with thirteen films in the running, alongside the long-standing gala, vision and documentary strands.

items.headline: Bank counters keep short hours — and today they are shut
items.body: Korean bank branches are generally open 09:00 to 16:00 on weekdays only, so on a public holiday like today there is no counter service; Korea Post banking runs to 16:30. Notes come in 1,000, 5,000, 10,000 and 50,000 won, and cards are taken almost everywhere — hotels, department stores and ordinary shops. To change foreign currency you need a bank or an authorised exchange centre, and very old notes are not always accepted.

items.headline: Baseball’s regular season ends tomorrow, and then the ladder starts
items.body: The KBO regular season, which started on 28 March, ends on Wednesday 7 October, after the league squeezed 105 rescheduled and rained-off games into the run-in. Five of the ten clubs then go into a step-ladder postseason that opens with a wild-card series and finishes in the Korean Series. Weekday games have been starting at 6:30 pm, weekend and holiday games earlier in the afternoon.

items.headline: Korea rents you a room for almost anything
items.body: A lot of Korean leisure happens in a private room you rent by the hour: a noraebang for singing, a PC room for gaming, a board-game cafe with tens of thousands of games, an escape room, a comic-book cafe with honeycomb booths, even a sauna room for one or two. The Hongdae noraebang used in “Hospital Playlist” is a two-storey building of nothing but singing rooms. Nobody outside the room is watching, which is the whole point.

items.headline: Two new dramas land on Friday, both twelve episodes
items.body: “Doctor X” arrives on 9 October and runs Fridays and Saturdays, with Kim Ji Won as a surgeon who proves herself with a scalpel and makes enemies of the hospital hierarchy. The same day brings “Take Charge of My Heart” with Kim Young Kwang and Chae Soo Bin, in which a man living with an artificial heart meets a woman who can generate electricity.

items.headline: Wear a hanbok and the palaces let you in free
items.body: Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, Changgyeonggung and Deoksugung all waive admission for anyone wearing hanbok, which is why the streets by the palace gates are full of people in rented silk. The shops there carry both traditional and modern cuts and usually include hair and accessories. This is a good week for it — the palaces are running their autumn festival from today until Sunday.

items.headline: Jazz takes over an island in Gapyeong from tomorrow
items.body: The 23rd Jarasum Jazz Festival runs from 9 to 11 October on Jara Island and around Gapyeong in Gyeonggi Province, with 39 acts on the bill — among them the drummer Nate Smith, back after seventeen years, and the pianist Tigran Hamasyan. France is this year’s focus country, marking 140 years of relations. Primary-school children get in free, and you can bring your dog.

items.headline: The subway rules that catch people out
items.body: Transfers between lines are free as long as you do not tap out through a gate, so plan the whole route inside the system rather than above it. A single-journey ticket costs a 500-won deposit on top of the fare, which you get back by feeding the card into a refund machine before you leave the station. Lines are colour-coded, most stations have lockers, and the Shinbundang Line charges extra for part of its route.

items.headline: Hangul Day: the king who made the alphabet gets a party at his tomb
items.body: Today and tomorrow the royal tomb of King Sejong in Yeoju hosts a free Hangul Day festival for the 580th anniversary of the alphabet’s proclamation, with a “five senses Hangul playground” of six hands-on activities — brush calligraphy, type design, paper lanterns — two calligraphy exhibitions and small outdoor concerts. Children’s shows run at 11 am, 2 pm and 4 pm today. Everything is free and seating is first come, first served.

items.headline: Eight more Korean words are now in the Oxford English Dictionary
items.body: In January the Oxford English Dictionary took in ramyeon, haenyeo, seonbae, bingsu, jjimjilbang, ajumma, officetel and Korean barbecue — the second year running that it has added Korean words, after dalgona, maknae and tteokbokki the year before. Useful to know that some of the Korean you are learning no longer needs translating.

items.headline: A pickpocket turns spy in the weekend drama starting today
items.body: “100 Days of Deception” begins today and airs Saturdays and Sundays over sixteen episodes, with Kim You Jung as a gifted pickpocket who ends up spying for the independence army under Japanese rule, alongside Park Jin Young and Kim Hyun Joo. If you have been watching period dramas for the silk and the swords, this one is set much closer to now.

items.headline: Next month the whole country makes kimchi at once
items.body: Kimjang is the November ritual of making winter kimchi together: cabbage soaked in salt water, then a paste of chilli flakes, garlic, ginger and radish worked in by hand, leaf by leaf. An extended family may put up around fifty heads of cabbage, enough for three or four months, and boxes of it go out to relatives, neighbours and colleagues. UNESCO listed the practice in 2013 — not the recipe, the sharing.

items.headline: Last day at the palaces — and every programme in the festival is free
items.body: The autumn K-Royal Culture Festival closes tonight after five days across Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, Deoksugung, Changgyeonggung and Jongmyo Shrine, with programmes such as an evening hanbok stroll at Gyeongbokgung and a reconstruction of royal daily life at Changgyeonggung. All of it is free of charge. If you miss it, the palaces themselves are open the rest of the year.

items.headline: On a Sunday a market can be half shut — except the food
items.body: Gwangjang Market in Jongno was the first permanent market in Korea, and it still sells silk, hanbok fabric, bedding, handicrafts and dried goods from 9 am to 6 pm. It closes on Sundays — but the food street does not, and that part runs until about 11 pm every day. Its name means roughly “gather from afar and keep it all together”.

items.headline: Seoraksan is a week away from its best colour
items.body: The first autumn leaves were recorded on Seoraksan on 28 September, and the Korea Forest Service’s forecast puts the peak there around 20 October, with Sokrisan following on 28 October, Naejangsan on 4 November and Hallasan on 6 November. Odaesan is expected to turn at about the same time as Seorak. If you want red mountains rather than green ones, the next fortnight is the window in the north-east.

items.headline: The price on the menu is the price you pay
items.body: Since 2013 Korean law has required restaurant menu prices to include tax and any service charge, so the number you see is the number on the bill. Tipping is not expected — wages are paid by the employer — though handing a tip to someone is not illegal. A tip jar or a kiosk that asks for one is unusual enough to cause complaints.

items.headline: Jinju’s lanterns stay on the river until Sunday
items.body: The Namgang Yudeung Festival in Jinju runs until 18 October, with lanterns floating on the Namgang River by Jinju Fortress under this year’s theme, “carrying peace on the river of history”. The culture ministry has named it one of its world festivals for 2026–2028, and this year’s drone shows use more than 950 drones. The 75th Gaecheon Art Festival runs alongside it and also ends on Sunday.

items.headline: Birthday breakfast is seaweed soup, and it is for your mother
items.body: Miyeokguk — brown seaweed simmered with beef and seasoned with soy sauce — is the first meal served to a woman after she gives birth. That is why Koreans eat it on their birthdays: a bowl of the same soup is a way of remembering the person who went through the birth. If a Korean friend makes you seaweed soup on your birthday, that is the gesture.

items.headline: Autumn baseball starts tonight with the wild-card game
items.body: The KBO postseason opens today with the wild-card round, played at the fourth-placed team’s ground: one win or even a draw sends the fourth-placed side through, while the fifth-placed side has to win twice. KT Wiz finished top and wait in the Korean Series. This year there are no rain-shortened games — a game interrupted by rain is suspended and finished later.

items.headline: Why Korean chopsticks are metal, flat and heavy
items.body: Most of East Asia eats with wooden or bamboo chopsticks, but Korea uses flat metal ones, usually stainless steel. They are heavier and more slippery than you are used to, but they stand up to hot soups and red marinades without staining. They come with a metal spoon, and the pair has its own name, sujeo — a reminder that much of Asia does not put a spoon on the table at all.

items.headline: Chuncheon is cooking its two famous dishes cheaply until Sunday
items.body: The Chuncheon Makguksu and Dakgalbi Festival runs from 14 to 18 October, with twelve dakgalbi restaurants and eight makguksu restaurants from the city setting up together. Dakgalbi, spicy chicken stir-fried on an iron pan, is 9,900 won a serving; makguksu, cold buckwheat noodles, is 6,900 won.

items.headline: Korean rubbish goes in three piles, and chicken bones are not food
items.body: Households in Korea split waste into general rubbish, food waste and recyclables, and put it out only during set collection hours. The rules that catch newcomers: chicken bones go in general waste, not food waste; labels come off plastic bottles; and glass bottles are separated from their caps. If you are staying in an apartment, ask the building manager how your block does it.

items.headline: A seedless persimmon gets its own three-day festival
items.body: The Cheongdo Bansi Festival runs from today until Sunday around the Cheongdo outdoor theatre in North Gyeongsang, celebrating bansi, the county’s flat, seedless persimmon. It shares the weekend with the Cheongdo World Comedy Art Festival, so expect acrobats, magic and circus acts between the fruit stalls, and the singer K.Will on Saturday. Free shuttle buses run every twenty minutes, including from Cheongdo Station.

items.headline: At the jjimjilbang, the egg and the rice punch are the ritual
items.body: The classic jjimjilbang snack is a roasted egg with a cup of sikhye, a cold sweet rice drink, bought at the snack bar inside. You do not need cash: the locker key on your wrist runs a tab for snacks and massage chairs, and you settle it at the counter when you leave. Start in the cooler 30–40°C rooms and keep to about twenty minutes in anything above 60°C.

items.headline: Grand Mint Festival fills Olympic Park this weekend
items.body: Grand Mint Festival takes over Olympic Park today and tomorrow across four stages. Among the first names announced, Saturday has Jang Ki-ha, Peppertones and Lee Seung-yoon, and Sunday has CNBLUE, Roy Kim and Yunha. Tickets have been sold through NOL, YES24 and Naver.

items.headline: Haneul Park’s silver-grass festival opens today
items.body: The 25th Seoul Eulalia Festival runs from today to 23 October on Haneul Park in World Cup Park, open 10 am to 9 pm, when the hilltop is covered in silver grass. From World Cup Stadium or Mapo-gu Office station on Line 6 it is about a 40-minute walk, or you can take the small electric shuttle from the Nanjicheon Park car park. The city asks visitors to come by public transport.

items.headline: Yoga on a closed bridge over the Han this afternoon
items.body: Jamsugyo Bridge is closed to cars again today for the Sunday festival on the bridge and Banpo Hangang Park, 2 pm to 10 pm, and this week’s programme is yoga, stretching and meditation. Only one more Sunday remains this autumn, and it is the last season before the bridge is turned over to pedestrians for good in the second half of 2027.

items.headline: Show your passport and the tax comes off at the till
items.body: Visitors staying under six months can reclaim tax on purchases of 15,000 won or more at tax-refund shops. Many shops deduct it on the spot if you show your passport, for single purchases under 1 million won and up to 5 million won across the trip; otherwise you keep the voucher and claim at the airport or a downtown kiosk. Goods have to leave the country unused within three months.

items.headline: Seoraksan turns today, and the colour starts moving south
items.body: The Korea Forest Service’s 2026 foliage peak map puts Seoraksan at its best today and Odaesan tomorrow, with the whole central region peaking between now and 1 November. Bukhansan above Seoul is due around 1 November and Naejangsan in the south on the 4th. Weekday walks are the quiet ones — the mountain buses fill up on Saturdays.

items.headline: You can book a night in a mountain temple
items.body: Templestay puts visitors up overnight at Buddhist temples across the country, around 170 of them. Programmes range from the full experience — seated meditation, the formal bowl meal, tea with a monk, making prayer beads — to a rest stay with nothing scheduled at all. Day visits are available too, and the site has an English version you can book from.

items.headline: Autumn baseball is on, and the deciding series is next month
items.body: The KBO postseason opened on 14 October with the wild card game. The semi-playoff and playoff are best-of-five, and the Korean Series — best-of-seven — starts on 2 November, so this week’s games decide who reaches it. Korean crowds sing a different chant for every batter, which is half the reason to go.

items.headline: When the subway stops, the N buses keep going
items.body: Seoul’s night buses carry an N for night plus two digits, and they run from midnight to about 5 am, every 30 to 50 minutes, on routes that cross the whole city. The city reckons riders save around 7,000 won a head against a late-night taxi, which is the real argument for waiting at the stop.

items.headline: The garden show at Seoul Forest closes next Tuesday
items.body: The 2026 Seoul International Garden Show has been open since 1 May — 167 gardens over 90,000 square metres, the longest run the city has staged at 180 days — and it ends on 27 October. Entry is free, and the gardens spill out of Seoul Forest into the streets of Seongsu-dong.

items.headline: The small dishes are free, and so are the refills
items.body: Every Korean meal arrives with banchan, the little side dishes set in the middle of the table, and in most restaurants you can ask for more at no charge — increasingly from a self-service bar by the wall. Ingredient prices have restaurant owners arguing about whether free refills can last, so enjoy them while the argument runs.

items.headline: Two Netflix dramas are still dropping episodes this week
items.body: "Doctor X", twelve episodes about a surgeon who will not follow hospital rules, and "100 Days of Deception", sixteen episodes about a pickpocket sent undercover during the occupation, both started in early October and are still releasing weekly. Starting one now means you catch up in time for the finale rather than after it.

items.headline: Ill at night? Call 1339 before you go looking for a hospital
items.body: 1339 is a 24-hour medical line that will tell you whether your symptoms need an emergency room, with an interpreter brought onto the call; you can reach it through KakaoTalk instead of paying for the call. Districts also designate late-night pharmacies that stay open to midnight or beyond, and convenience stores sell basic fever, cold and stomach medicine at any hour.

items.headline: Food trucks compete by the river at Ttukseom from today
items.body: The Road Chef Hangang, a street-food contest, runs today to Sunday at the pool in Ttukseom Hangang Park. It is part of the autumn Hangang Festival, which has been running since 17 October across seven riverside parks and finishes on the 25th.

items.headline: Four numbers worth keeping in your phone
items.body: 112 is police, 119 is fire and ambulance, 1339 is medical advice, and 1330 is the travel hotline — eight languages, and it will interpret for you on a three-way call with a taxi driver or a shop. Large hospitals also run international health care centres with English-speaking staff, generally on weekdays only.

items.headline: The city puts its library back out on the square today
items.body: Seoul’s outdoor libraries run Friday to Sunday through the autumn at three places — Seoul Plaza, Gwanghwamun Square and the Cheonggyecheon stream — with deckchairs, borrowed books and small performances. Hours shift between 11 am to 6 pm and 4 pm to 10 pm depending on the weather, so check before heading over in the evening.

items.headline: How to read a Korean address
items.body: An address is a road name plus a building number. A daero has more than eight lanes, a ro seven or fewer, and a gil is a small street off one of them. Numbers run west to east and south to north, odd on the left and even on the right, so the number alone tells you roughly how far along you are. Old lot-number addresses still get delivered, and juso.go.kr converts between the two.

items.headline: The last car-free Sunday on Jamsugyo is today
items.body: Jamsugyo Bridge shuts to traffic from noon to midnight for the eighth and final Sunday of the autumn programme, with the festival itself running 2 pm to 10 pm on the bridge and in Banpo Hangang Park. The city plans to hand the bridge to pedestrians for good in the second half of 2027, so this is the last autumn of the arrangement.

items.headline: The government runs a free Korean school online
items.body: The King Sejong Institute gives its course material away on its Nuri site — videos, textbooks, grammar guides, even comics about Korean food — with a short placement test to find your level. Free online classes open for some countries each term, and there are vocabulary apps and a YouTube channel alongside. Sign up from a computer; the registration does not work well on a phone.

items.headline: Hampyeong fills a park with chrysanthemums until 8 November
items.body: The National Chrysanthemum Festival in Hampyeong, South Jeolla, opened on 23 October at Hampyeong Expo Park and runs for 17 days. This year’s theme is a garden of myths, built from giant flower sculptures — the county breeds several of its own chrysanthemum varieties for them.

items.headline: At a Korean table, the youngest pours
items.body: At a work dinner the younger people pour for the older ones, starting with the most senior, holding the bottle with both hands or with the left hand resting on the right arm. Take a glass from a senior with both hands and keep yours a little lower when you clink. If you do not drink, accept the first glass and touch it to your lips — that is polite enough.

items.headline: The leaves around Seoul are at their best from now
items.body: The 2026 foliage map from the Korea Tourism Organization and the Korea National Arboretum puts the peak for the capital region and Gangwon in late October, with the Gyeongsang and Jeolla provinces following in early to mid November. If you are in Seoul this week, you do not need to travel far for the colour.

items.headline: Wait for the oldest person to start eating
items.body: Starting your meal before the older people at the table is considered rude. Spoons and chopsticks are often kept in a box or drawer at the table, and whoever reaches in first sets them out for everyone, not just themselves — the same goes for pouring the water. Stews often come in one big pot that the whole table shares.

items.headline: Lee Chang-dong’s new film reaches Netflix a week on Friday
items.body: "Possible Love", the director’s first feature since "Burning", streams worldwide from 6 November. Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung and Cho Yeo-jeong play two married couples whose lives cross when one of them sets out to make a documentary about the other. It is Korea’s entry for the international feature Oscar.

items.headline: Shoes come off at the door
items.body: In Korea shoes come off at the entrance to a home, and at restaurants with floor seating too. The habit comes from a floor-centred life: people traditionally sat and slept on the floor, and many houses had no chairs, sofas or beds. Wear socks you are happy to show.

items.headline: A picnic on Namsan this Friday and Saturday evening
items.body: The Namsan Night Festival runs Namsan Campnic at Baekbeom Square on Friday and Saturday evenings, 5 pm to 10 pm, with 100 spots a night for up to four people each. Spots are booked in advance on the festival site with a 10,000-won deposit that is refunded after you turn up. The festival carries on at weekends until 14 November.

items.headline: When it turns cold, the fish-shaped bread comes out
items.body: Bungeoppang, a fish-shaped pastry usually filled with red bean or custard, appears at street stalls and food trucks as soon as the weather turns. Stalls come and go, so Koreans track them on crowdsourced maps in the Karrot neighbourhood app, and newer stalls sell cheese, pizza and even kimchi fillings.

source.name: Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism

items.headline: Busan catches mackerel by hand on Songdo Beach from today
items.body: The Busan Mackerel Festival runs today to Sunday, 10 am to 9 pm, at Songdo Beach in Seo-gu, and entry is free. You can try catching a mackerel with your bare hands, watch a surprise auction, tour the city’s main fish market, and eat your way through a mackerel food market.

source.name: Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism

items.headline: Late-night delivery now works on a foreign card
items.body: Baemin, the biggest delivery app, accepts foreign-issued credit cards, Apple Pay, WeChat Pay and Alipay, and has had English, Chinese and Japanese menus since February. Orders from visitors more than quadrupled in the first half of this year, and fried chicken was what they ordered most.

source.name: The Korea Herald via Asia News Network

items.headline: Miryang holds a spicy-food festival this weekend
items.body: The Miryang Spicy Food Festival runs today and tomorrow, 11 am to 9 pm, along the Miryang riverside in South Gyeongsang, with free entry. There are spicy-food challenges and a Scoville scale to fill in, and Samyang, the maker of Buldak noodles, runs a booth.

source.name: Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism

items.headline: An hour on a Seoul city bike costs 1,000 won
items.body: Ttareungyi, Seoul’s public bike service, has around 45,000 bikes at some 2,800 stations. An hour costs 1,000 won and two hours 2,000 won, and you can return the bike at any station. The riverside paths along the Han are the easy place to start.

items.headline: Busan’s fireworks are next Saturday
items.body: The 21st Busan Fireworks Festival is on Saturday 7 November over Gwangalli Beach and Gwangan Bridge, with events running from 1 pm to 8 pm. Some of the seating is paid, so check busanfireworks.com for tickets — and if you want to stay over, book now rather than next week.

source.name: Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism

items.headline: Bunsik is the cheap snack food Korea runs on
items.body: Bunsik literally means food made with flour, and it covers the snack-bar menu: tteokbokki, gimbap, sundae, fish-cake skewers and ramyeon. It spread after the Korean War, when rice was short and the government spent years pushing flour instead. A bunsikjip sign means a quick, cheap meal.
